reading.translation:
The Greeks were marching through Armenia. There was much snow, and the cold was severe. The soldiers and pack animals struggled; not all endured the hardship.

Many of the pack animals died, and people died too. Not only soldiers but also enslaved people were in the snow. The hardship was shared, but their strength was not equal.

Those who arrived first were keeping a fire burning. Those who came later approached the fire. The first arrivals demanded food and only then admitted the others.

On the next day the men were marching again. Some fell and remained behind. Xenophon stopped beside the weak men; he did not immediately recognize their condition.

A man recognized the condition and told Xenophon. Xenophon went to the pack animals and looked for food. Those who were strong carried the food to the weak.

The weak men ate, then got up and continued marching. Words alone did not save them. For they needed nourishment. Here care brought benefit to their companions.

blocks.title: πόνος is not the whole story
body: πόνος can mean toil, exertion, or hardship. καρτερία names endurance. Their association in moral writing does not mean that more suffering always produces more virtue.
Add βοήθεια, “help,” to the pair. This episode asks who makes continued movement possible. A vocabulary list can become a map of relationships, not merely a set of private qualities.

sections.title: 1. Athematic second aorists
body: Some second aorists attach endings directly to a root, without a thematic ο/ε vowel. Recognize ἔβην from βαίνω and ἔστην from ἵστημι. Like other aorist indicatives, they carry an augment and present a past event as a whole.
Their meaning must be learned with their principal parts. ἔβην means “I went/stepped”; ἔστην means “I stood,” not “I made someone stand.” The full transitive contrast returns in Lesson 35.

sections.title: 2. Aorist infinitives, participles, commands
body: Outside the indicative, the aorist does not take an augment. βῆναι is an infinitive; βάς is a masculine nominative singular participle. Its feminine is βᾶσα, neuter βάν. The genitive βάντος reveals the -ντ- stem.

Aorist commands present the requested action as a whole: βῆθι, “go!” Compare στῆθι, “stand!” Aorist participles normally show action prior to the main verb, though context determines the precise relation.

sections.title: 3. Recognizing -εσ- nouns in difficult terrain
body: Apply the -εσ- noun pattern to the physical world: τὸ ὄρος, τοῦ ὄρους, “mountain”; τὸ βάθος, τοῦ βάθους, “depth.” τὸ χεῖλος, τοῦ χείλους can mean a lip or an edge. The genitive -ους comes from contraction, not second declension.
Nominative and accusative neuter forms coincide. τὰ ὄρη can therefore be a subject or object; context decides. After ἐν, τοῖς ὄρεσιν is dative plural.

sections.title: 4. Reading events, background, and physical limits
body: A narrative may set snow and exhaustion in the background with imperfects, then use aorists for particular decisions. A participle can compress one action into the frame of another. Name the subject of each action rather than treating all soldiers as doing the same thing.

Vocabulary also carries the argument. Hunger and cold are physical conditions, not proof of a moral defect. In the reading, provision of food belongs to competent leadership. Grammar helps us see who notices, moves, gives, and recovers.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Anabasis
body: The Anabasis tells of Cyrus the Younger’s expedition and the Greek army’s difficult return after his death. Xenophon participated in the expedition and later became one of its leaders. The narrative often names him in the third person, a literary choice that does not remove his stake in the story.

Book 4 carries the army through harsh winter conditions in Armenia. Our selection uses 4.5.3–9, including exhaustion and the discovery that food could help men who could no longer continue. We simplify the sequence and language; we do not diagnose every individual from a modern medical standpoint.

sections.title: A landscape that changes the task
body: An army needs more than courage when snow, cold, distance, and hunger interrupt movement. The same ground can demand different decisions as supplies and strength change. A command to march cannot manufacture energy.

Read the banner for the care being offered, not as a precise reconstruction of one documented face or campsite. Then list the practical questions a leader needs answered: who can move, what food exists, and how can it reach those who need it?

sections.title: Recognizing a limit is a skill
body: Xenophon’s account gives us a useful counterweight to the Heracles allegory. In the story of choice, effort leads toward a worthwhile aim. Here, exhausted people need support before further effort is possible.

Do not turn bodily collapse into a verdict on character. Ask what the leader notices and changes. Competence includes distinguishing unwillingness from inability; the passage also reminds us that a leader’s own narrative may present his decisions favorably.

sections.title: Make an action map
body: Draw three boxes: notice, provide, move. Place an appropriate Greek verb under each, marking whether it gives background or an event viewed as a whole. Add the person who performs the action.
Your map should show care as an action, not an interruption to the “real” story. End with one sentence explaining how this episode changes your definition of endurance.
